e.etymology: Matches the senna plant, a yellow-flowered shrub whose name comes from Arabic sana. It is also the surname of Brazilian racing driver Ayrton Senna, and has long been a popular girls' name in the Netherlands.

assoc.t: senna, a common over-the-counter herbal laxative
Senna, a champion in League of Legends

e.note: Senna is sold in every US pharmacy as an herbal laxative, and racing fans will think of Ayrton Senna.

e.etymology: A recent American coinage that joins Mae to the -lani ending of Hawaiian names such as Leilani and Kailani, where lani means 'sky, heaven'.

e.meaning: the Americas, named for Amerigo Vespucci
e.etymology: From New Latin America, the name a 1507 map gave the New World in honor of explorer Amerigo Vespucci. Amerigo is the Italian form of a Germanic name related to Henry and Emmerich.
namesakes: America Ferrera (actress, Ugly Betty and Barbie)

assoc.t: the United States, and the American continents

e.note: Shares its name with the country, so it can read as a patriotic statement; as América it is a familiar Spanish name.

e.meaning: short for Ricardo, 'brave ruler'; also Spanish for rich
e.etymology: A short form of Ricardo, Federico and Enrico, Romance forms of Germanic names that all contain ric, 'ruler, power'. Rico is also the Spanish word for rich or delicious.
namesakes: Rico Rodriguez (actor, Manny on Modern Family)

assoc.t: Rico, the penguin in the Madagascar films

e.note: RICO is the well-known federal racketeering law, as in 'a RICO charge'.

e.etymology: A Russian pet form of Sofya (Sophia), from Greek sophia, 'wisdom'. English speakers met it through 19th-century Russian novels such as Crime and Punishment and War and Peace and adopted it in the early 1900s.
A pet form of Abigail, from Hebrew Avigayil, 'my father's joy'. This spelling was the usual one in 19th-century America; it has occasionally also been short for Albert or Abbott.
namesakes: Abbie Hoffman (1960s activist and Yippie leader)

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English lind, 'linden (lime) tree', plus dun, 'hill'. Lyndon is a village in Rutland. President Lyndon B. Johnson made it familiar as a first name.
A respelling of Jett with the h of Rhett. Jett comes from jet, the glossy black gemstone, a word later borrowed for the jet aircraft; it is also an English surname.
A modern American coinage joining the Tay- sound of Taylor to the popular -lynn ending, in the pattern of Raelynn and Jaelyn.
From Arabic jasir, 'bold, courageous', from the verb jasara, 'to dare'. In the United States it is used mostly in African American and Muslim families.
A recent spelling of Kayson, a modern American name made in the pattern of Jason, Mason and Grayson. The Kai- spelling borrows the look of Kai.
A pet form of Joan, the medieval English feminine of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. In Finland Joni is a separate boys' name, a form of John.
namesakes: Joni Eareckson Tada (Christian author and speaker)

e.etymology: Feminine of Darius, the Greek form of the Old Persian royal name Darayavahush, 'he who holds firm the good'. Saint Daria of Rome, a 3rd-century martyr, carried it across Christian Europe.
namesakes: Daria Morgendorffer (title character of MTV's Daria)

assoc.t: Daria, deadpan teen of the 1990s MTV cartoon

e.etymology: The Armenian form of Leon, borrowed from Greek leon, 'lion', and borne by medieval Armenian kings. Americans know it from Levon Helm of The Band and from Elton John's 1971 song Levon.
namesakes: Levon Helm (drummer and singer of The Band)

e.etymology: A short form of Nathan, Hebrew Natan, 'he gave', and of Nathaniel, 'God has given'. Long a nickname, it is now also registered as a name in its own right.
From Persian arman, 'longing, heartfelt wish, ideal', a word carried into Urdu, Hindi and Punjabi. The double a is the usual South Asian spelling; Arman is also an Armenian and Kazakh name.
The pet name Victor Hugo gave the heroine of Les Miserables (1862), whose real name is Euphrasie. It is generally explained as French chosette, 'little thing'.
namesakes: Cosette (heroine of Victor Hugo's Les Miserables)

assoc.t: Cosette, the orphan girl of Les Miserables

e.etymology: A spelling of Sunny, the English word used as a cheerful given name and nickname.

assoc.t: Sunni Islam, the largest branch of Islam

e.note: Written this way it is the word for the largest branch of Islam (said SOO-nee), which many readers will see first.

e.etymology: A recent name used mainly in Hispanic families in the United States and Latin America, alongside Nashla and Nashley. Its source is not established; the sound follows Ashley.
An African American coinage of the late 1980s that adds the -te ending of Dante to Devon. It spread after DeVante Swing of the R&B group Jodeci became famous in the early 1990s.
An African American spelling of Dion, a Greek name that was also the medieval short form of Dionysius, the source of Dennis. Deion Sanders made this spelling famous in the 1990s.
namesakes: Deion Sanders (NFL Hall of Famer and college football coach)
Deion Branch (Super Bowl MVP wide receiver)

assoc.t: Deion Sanders, 'Prime Time' NFL star and coach

e.etymology: In Hindi jiya is a poetic word for the heart or soul, familiar from Bollywood song lyrics, and is used as a girls' name. The same spelling also renders the Arabic-derived name Zia, 'radiance'.
A spelling of Lilith, Hebrew Lilit, from Akkadian lilitu, a female night spirit. In medieval Jewish legend Lilith is Adam's first wife, who left Eden rather than obey him.
namesakes: Lilith Sternin (Frasier's ex-wife on Cheers and Frasier)

assoc.t: Lilith, night demon and Adam's first wife in Jewish lore

e.note: Lilith is a night demon in Jewish folklore; some hear the name as dark, others as a feminist emblem.

e.etymology: The English word valley, from Old French valee and Latin vallis, used as a nature name. Vallie was a girls' name a century ago, as a pet form of Valerie and Valentine.

assoc.t: the Valley, LA's San Fernando Valley of 'Valley girl' fame

e.etymology: The Russian pet form of Mikhail (Michael), made from the first syllable plus the affectionate ending -sha; Michael is Hebrew for 'who is like God?'. English speakers adopted it as a full name, mostly for girls.
e.note: In Russia Misha is a boys' nickname, the equivalent of Mike; in the US it is given mostly to girls.

e.etymology: A spelling of Charlie, the pet form of Charles and of Charlotte and Charlene. Charles goes back to Germanic karl, 'free man'.
From Arabic sa'id, 'happy, lucky, blessed', from the verb sa'ada, 'to be fortunate'. One of the most widespread Arabic boys' names, also spelled Saeed.
e.note: Spelled like the English word 'said', so it is often misread as SED.

e.etymology: An African American name of the 1970s, probably a blend of Jamal and Lamar.
In American use a phonetic spelling of Aaron for boys and of Erin for girls. Aaron is the biblical brother of Moses; Erin comes from the Irish word for Ireland.
A spelling of Shiloh, the town where the Israelites kept the tabernacle before Jerusalem. The Hebrew is often read as 'tranquil'. The 1862 Civil War battle was named for a Shiloh church in Tennessee.

assoc.t: Battle of Shiloh, 1862 Civil War battle in Tennessee
Shiloh, the beagle of the 1991 children's novel

e.etymology: From Spanish blanca, 'white, fair', a word of Germanic origin. It was a royal name in medieval Navarre and Castile and matches French Blanche and Italian Bianca.
A spelling of Corbin, an Anglo-Norman surname from corb, 'crow, raven', first a nickname for someone dark-haired. It may also shorten Corbinian, an 8th-century Frankish saint.

assoc.t: Jeremy Corbyn, former leader of Britain's Labour Party
